source_text: III. Martianus ait: Quae te philosophiae disputatio vana decepit? sperne invisibilia; potius deos veros quos aspicis recognosce. respondit Achatius: Qui sunt dii quibus sacrificare me praecipis? Martianus ait: Apollini servatori nostro, famis et pestilentiae depulsori, per quem omnis mundus servatur [et — scan οὗ] regitur. respondit Achatius: Illi vestro, ut putatis, interpreti? qui infelix cum puellae amore flagraret currebat attonitus, ignarus perditurum se optatissimam praedam. apertum est itaque quia nec divinus fuit qui ista nescivit, nec deus quem puella decepit. nec hic solum dolores excepit, sed crudelior illum damno mox fortuna multavit. nam ut erat turpis in pueros, forma Hyacinthi cuiusdam captus, ut bene nostis, incaluit et miser atque ignarus futuri disco illum quem optabat videre occidit. qui cum Neptuno aliquando servivit, ipsi qui aliena pecora servavit, huic sacrificare me praecipis? an Aesculapio fulminato, an adulterae Veneri et [porientis — unreadable; sense: and the rest of that sort] ceteris sacrificium impendam? vel ob huius vitae exitum adorabo ego eos quos non dignor imitari? quos contemno, quos accuso, quos horreo; quorum facta nunc si quis admittat, num severitatem legis vestrae poterit effugere? et modo in aliis colitis quae in aliis vindicatis? Martianus ait: Christianorum consuetudo est multa in deos nostros maledicta confingere. propterea te venire mecum ad Iovem Iunonemque praecipio, ut simul celebrantes dulce convivium numinibus quae sunt digna reddamus. respondit Achatius: Quomodo hic sacrificabo illi cuius sepulcrum esse constat in Creta? numquid resurrexit a mortuis?
pass_a_gloss: Martianus says: What empty philosophical argument misled you? Throw away unseen things; rather recognize the true gods whom you look at. Achatius answers: Who are the gods to whom you order me to sacrifice? Martianus says: To Apollo our preserver, averter of hunger and plague, through whom the whole world is kept safe and ruled. Achatius answers: To that interpreter of yours, as you think, who, wretched, while he burned with love for a girl, ran frenzied, not knowing that he would lose his most desired prey? It is plain therefore that he was neither prophetic who did not know these things, nor god whom a girl tricked. Nor did he suffer pains only here, but soon a crueler fortune punished him with loss. For as one shameful toward boys, seized by the beauty of a certain Hyacinth, as you well know, he grew hot and, wretched and ignorant of the future, killed with a discus him whom he desired to look upon. When he once served as a slave together with Neptune, he himself who guarded another's flocks — to this one do you order me to sacrifice? Or shall I spend sacrifice on lightning-struck Aesculapius, or on adulterous Venus and the rest? Or for the sake of this life's outcome shall I worship those whom I do not deem worthy to imitate? Whom I despise, whom I accuse, at whom I shudder; if anyone now should commit their deeds, will he be able to escape the severity of your law? And do you now worship in some beings what you punish in others? Martianus says: It is the habit of Christians to invent many curses against our gods. Therefore I order you to come with me to Jupiter and Juno, so that feasting together we may render to the divine powers things worthy of them. Achatius answers: How shall I sacrifice here to him whose tomb is agreed to be in Crete? Did he rise from the dead?
pass_b_english: Martianus said: What vain philosophical disputation deceived you?
Spurn invisible things; acknowledge instead the true gods whom you behold.
Achatius answered: Who are the gods to whom you bid me sacrifice?
Martianus said: To Apollo our preserver, the averter of famine and pestilence, through whom the whole world is kept safe and governed.
Achatius answered: To that oracle-mouth of yours, as you deem him?
Unhappy creature, while he blazed with love for a girl he ran distracted, ignorant that he would lose his most longed-for prize.
It is open therefore that he was neither divine who knew not these things, nor god whom a girl outwitted.
Nor did he meet with sorrows only there, but soon a crueller fortune punished him with loss.

For, being base in his love toward boys, taken as you well know with the beauty of a certain Hyacinthus, he burned and, wretched and ignorant of what was to come, slew with a discus the very one whom he longed to gaze upon.
Since he once slaved together with Neptune, he who himself kept another's flocks — to this fellow do you bid me sacrifice?
Or shall I bestow sacrifice upon lightning-blasted Aesculapius, or upon adulterous Venus and the rest of that sort?
Or shall I, for the sake of this life's passage, adore those whom I do not deem worthy to imitate?
Those whom I despise, whom I accuse, at whom I shudder; if anyone now committed their deeds, could he escape the severity of your law?
And do you now honor in some what you punish in others?
Martianus said: It is the custom of Christians to devise many curses against our gods.
Therefore I bid you come with me to Jupiter and Juno, that feasting together we may render to the powers what is due to them.
Achatius answered: How shall I sacrifice here to him whose tomb is agreed to stand in Crete?
Did he rise from the dead?

choices.term: Apollini servatori nostro, famis et pestilentiae depulsori
choices.english: to Apollo our preserver, the averter of famine and plague
choices.why: datives in apposition to Apollini, with genitives famis et pestilentiae depending on depulsori, so preserver/averter keeps the two titles distinct
rejected: to Apollo our saviour from famine and plague

choices.term: vel ob huius vitae exitum adorabo ego eos quos non dignor imitari?
choices.english: or shall I, for the sake of this life's course, worship those whom I do not think worthy to imitate?
choices.why: vel introduces the last rejected alternative and ob with accusative gives motive; dignor with infinitive expresses deemed unworthy, not inability
rejected: or shall I worship them to escape death?
